paper.title: RSA: Byzantine-Robust Stochastic Aggregation Methods for Distributed Learning from Heterogeneous Datasets

algorithm.name: RSA (l1, l2 and linfinity norm variants)
citations: PDF p.3 Eq.(5): unsquared l1 distance penalty added to each regular local objective.
PDF p.3 Eqs.(7),(8): local stochastic gradient plus signed penalty; master regularizer plus summed signs of regular and Byzantine model messages.
PDF p.4 Algorithm 2: master broadcasts x0^k, workers send xi^k, then both update; all right-hand sides use iteration k states.
PDF p.4 Eqs.(9)-(11) and Proposition 1: general lp norm penalty and subgradient characterized by inner product equality and dual norm bound.
PDF pp.4-5 Assumptions 1-3: strong convexity, Lipschitz gradients, independent-in-time local sampling and bounded variance; heterogeneous distributions across workers allowed.
PDF p.5 Theorem 1: consensus optimum requires lambda >= max_i ||gradient E F(x_tilde_star,xi_i)||_b; short trajectories do not assert this condition.
assumptions: All oracle functions are deterministic strongly convex quadratic losses with identity Hessian; stochastic variance is zero and worker centers differ.
All updates are simultaneous from a shared old-state snapshot. The master receives current local models, not gradients, and does not identify or remove Byzantine senders.
lambda is positive. Step sizes are explicit finite-probe inputs; no convergence claim is made for these short schedules.

The p=infinity parameter is JSON string infinity as a configuration value; all expected values are numeric. A variant missing from an implementation should be reported unsupported, not silently replaced by another p.

No l1 coordinate difference is zero, no l2 difference vector is zero, and every infinity-norm difference has a unique maximum absolute coordinate. Thus no arbitrary subgradient choice affects expected results.
Paper Algorithm 2 does not define a generic stopping condition or API return shape; here the prescribed final master iterate is the observable output, consistent with p.5 evaluation using x0.

cases.purpose: Nonzero heterogeneous states, active l1 penalty, sign reversal after first step, master regularizer, saturated Byzantine influence and summed old-model aggregation.
cases.derivation:
At k=0 worker signs are (+,+),(-,+), while the Byzantine master sign is (-,+). Therefore S=(-1,-1). Worker 1 crosses below the master in both coordinates after the first update, so its next sign is (-,-) and S becomes (+,+). This distinguishes the synchronous old-state formula from using already-updated worker messages. The Byzantine message magnitude alternates 100, 1e9, 100; its sign remains (-,+) and hence its penalty contribution remains (-0.5,+0.5).

All loss functions are F_i(x)=0.5*||x-a_i||_2^2 and f0(x)=0.5*||x-c0||_2^2. Thus gradients are x-a_i and x-c0, with no stochastic noise. Define s_i=partial||x_i-x0||_p and b_j=partial||x0-z_j||_p from OLD states. Master sum S=-sum_i s_i+sum_j b_j. Then x_i_new=x_i-alpha*(x_i-a_i+lambda*s_i); x0_new=x0-alpha*(x0-c0+lambda*S). No division by worker count. Derivative fields at step t refer to state t-1; master and regular_workers at step t are post-update. Final output is the last master; regular local states are also required.

cases.purpose: Distinguish the unsquared Euclidean norm subgradient from elementwise signs, squared norm gradients, clipping and mean aggregation.
cases.derivation:
For p=2 and a nonzero difference v, Proposition 1 implies s=v/||v||2. Initially worker differences are (3,4),(-4,3), with norms 5,5, and the Byzantine master difference is (-6,8), norm 10. Thus s1=(0.6,0.8), s2=(-0.8,0.6), b=(-0.6,0.8), S=(-0.4,-0.6). On step 2 all subgradients are recomputed from the changed full vector differences; they are not cached.

All loss functions are F_i(x)=0.5*||x-a_i||_2^2 and f0(x)=0.5*||x-c0||_2^2. Thus gradients are x-a_i and x-c0, with no stochastic noise. No division by worker count. Derivative fields at step t refer to state t-1; master and regular_workers at step t are post-update. Final output is the last master; regular local states are also required.

cases.purpose: Check the general-p variant: infinity-norm subgradient uses the signed uniquely largest absolute coordinate, with all other coordinates zero.
cases.derivation:
For p=infinity, the dual norm in Proposition 1 is l1. At a uniquely largest absolute coordinate, the unique subgradient is its signed coordinate basis vector. Initially v1=(3,1), v2=(-1,4), and vB=(-10,-2), so s1=(1,0),s2=(0,1),b=(-1,0),S=(-2,-1). On step 2 differences are (1.9,1.1),(-0.4,2.8),(-10,-1.7), so the same unique supporting coordinates remain.

All loss functions are F_i(x)=0.5*||x-a_i||_2^2 and f0(x)=0.5*||x-c0||_2^2. Thus gradients are x-a_i and x-c0, with no stochastic noise. Define s_i=partial||x_i-x0||_p and b_j=partial||x0-z_j||_p from OLD states. Master sum S=-sum_i s_i+sum_j b_j. Then x_i_new=x_i-alpha*(x_i-a_i+lambda*s_i); x0_new=x0-alpha*(x0-c0+lambda*S). No division by worker count. Derivative fields at step t refer to state t-1; master and regular_workers at step t are post-update. Final output is the last master; regular local states are also required.
